goals: Understand how optimization and regularization affect singular-value spectra and the effective rank of weight matrices.
Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.
Understand the geometry and practical language-model fine-tuning behavior of LoRA and other low-rank updates.
Evaluate tradeoffs among model quality, memory, throughput, and communication cost across model scales.
Build an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.11730.question: What matched baselines, experimental controls, and measured results are reported for effective rank, SVD-LLM compression, validation loss, GPU inference speedup, and robustness under label noise?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

passages.section: 3.1 Effective rank and why it matters
passages.text: Figure 1 : Validation loss (left) and mean effective rank of the weight matrices (right) during training of a 257 257 M-parameter LLaMA on FineWeb-Edu with Adam and spectral weight decay. We measure spectral concentration with the entropy-based effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] . For singular values σ 1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ σ r \sigma_{1}\geq\dots\geq\sigma_{r} and p i = σ i / ∑ j σ j p_{i}=\sigma_{i}/\sum_{j}\sigma_{j} , it is erank ( W ) = exp ( H ( p ) ) = exp ( − ∑ i p i log p i ) . \operatorname{erank}(W)=\exp\big(H(p)\big)=\exp\!\Big(-\sum_{i}p_{i}\log p_{i}\Big). (2) Effective rank ranges from 1 1 for a rank-one matrix to r = min ⁡ ( m , n ) r=\min(m,n) for a flat spectrum and decreases as the spectrum becomes more concentrated. We report a weighted mean across weight matrices, with weights min ⁡ ( m l , n l ) \min(m_{l},n_{l}) , excluding token embeddings and the output head. Figure 1 shows validation loss and mean effective rank during training of a 257 257 M-parameter LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] on FineWeb-Edu [ Penedo et al., 2024 ] with Adam and spectral weight decay. Appendix B.1 summarizes the pretraining configurations. Larger λ \lambda lowers effective rank, with a corresponding validation-loss trade-off. At the end of training, λ = 0.7 \lambda=0.7 reduces mean effective rank by a factor of 2.17 2.17 relative to λ = 0 \lambda=0 , with a 1.10 % 1.10\% increase in validation loss.

passages.section: 3.1 Effective rank and why it matters
passages.text: We use effective rank instead of stable rank, ‖ W ‖ F 2 / ‖ W ‖ 2 2 \|W\|_{F}^{2}/\|W\|_{2}^{2} , because it predicts a practical compression threshold. Truncating to ⌈ erank ⁡ ( W ) ⌉ \lceil\operatorname{erank}(W)\rceil preserves model quality, while lower ranks degrade it sharply (Figure 2 , right). Stable rank can remain near one when a single singular value dominates many active directions, so it does not capture this threshold. Figure 2 : Effective-rank profiles and compression of the λ = 1 \lambda=1 model. Left: effective rank as a percentage of full rank, grouped by layer type. Middle: the same ratio across transformer blocks. Right: validation loss after truncated SVD and SVD-LLM at different retained ranks. The vertical line marks the mean effective rank. Figure 3 : Compression and inference frontiers under validation-loss distortion budgets. Top: maximum compression rate relative to the best dense checkpoint at each scale. Bottom: maximum inference speedup.

selections.summary: Introduces decoupled nuclear-norm spectral weight decay to concentrate singular values and induce low-effective-rank weights. Across 124M–500M-parameter LLaMA models, it improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss, and improves clean-test accuracy under 60% label noise.
selections.relevance: Direct match for spectral regularization, effective rank, low-rank compressibility, SVD compression, and memorization under label noise.

evidence.quote: At 500M and a 4% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89× compression and a 1.18× GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14× and 1.01× after standard weight decay.
At the end of training, λ = 0.7 reduces mean effective rank by a factor of 2.17 relative to λ = 0, with a 1.10% increase in validation loss.

selections.summary: Presents sMuon, an efficient approximation to the Muon objective for low-rank adapters using linearization and least squares, with matmul-only implementation. It reports moderate improvements across supervised fine-tuning and a ReLoRA pretraining experiment.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses optimization for LoRA, low-rank parameterizations, Muon, and ReLoRA pretraining.

evidence.quote: Our method, sMuon (small Muon), performs favourably across SFT and a ReLoRA pretraining experiment.
we find overall that using Muon for low-rank fine-tuning provides moderate performance improvements.

selections.summary: Introduces NoRA, which normalizes LoRA down-projection matrices during training or only at initialization. The method is evaluated across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, where it reportedly improves convergence, stability, performance, and catastrophic-forgetting behavior without extra trainable parameters or inference computation.
selections.relevance: Strong fit for the geometry and optimization dynamics of LoRA and other low-rank updates.

evidence.quote: Because LoRA initializes the up-projection to zero, its early optimization dynamics are largely governed by the down-projection.
Across pretraining, supervised finetuning, and reinforcement learning, NoRA consistently accelerates convergence, improves performance and training stability, and mitigates catastrophic forgetting.

selections.summary: Proposes NorMuon, combining Muon's orthogonalization with neuron-wise adaptive normalization and an efficient distributed FSDP2 implementation. It targets non-uniform neuron update norms and practical scalability in LLM training.
selections.relevance: Relevant to Muon optimization, conditioning, distributed training, and efficiency at language-model scale.

evidence.quote: NorMuon addresses this imbalance by maintaining second-order momentum statistics for each neuron and applying row-wise normalization after orthogonalization.
To enable practical deployment at scale, we develop an efficient distributed implementation under the FSDP2 framework.

selections.summary: Introduces Context Language Models that treat context as a file the model can update, extending the approach to multi-agent contexts. The abstract reports improved accuracy and reduced FLOPs over context-management baselines, as well as gains from natural-language steering and skill optimization.
selections.relevance: Directly supports the user's goal of building an AI research-digest agent with explicit context management and tool-like context operations.

evidence.quote: We introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), language models that natively manage their own context.
This allows the model to learn what is most important to maintain in context, and naturally extends to multi-agent systems where multiple agent contexts coexist as files.

limitations: Only Spectral Weight Decay received full-text inspection. The remaining selections rely on abstracts, some of which are truncated or provide limited baseline and compute details.
Code availability and reproducibility were not independently checked.
X analysis was disabled, so no attention or popularity signal is included.
